concepts.title: 5.4 Organizational Framework — The McKinsey 7S Model
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 · RTP 5 · MTP 0 (10 atoms, 7 of them MCQs)
understand: **What the model is for.** ==**The McKinsey 7S Model refers to a tool that analyzes a company's "organizational design." The goal of the model is to depict how effectiveness can be achieved in an organization through the interactions of hard and soft elements. The McKinsey 7S Model focuses on how the "Soft Ss" and "Hard Ss" elements are interrelated, suggesting that modifying one aspect might have a ripple effect on the other elements in order to maintain an effective balance.**== The **ripple effect** phrase is the model's signature, and ICAI puts it into stems to signal that the 7S is wanted.

**The seven, split three and four.** ==**Hard elements are: Strategy, Structure, Systems. Soft elements are: Shared Values, Staff, Skill, Style.**== Three hard, four soft — get the count right, because one past-paper MCQ turns on nothing else.

**The study material's questionnaire framing of each element** — this is how the model is actually used, and PYQ May 2024 Q5(a) built its stem around preparing exactly such a questionnaire: ==**Strategy: What steps does the company intend to take to address current and future challenges? Structure: How is work divided, how do different departments work and collaborate? Systems: Which formal and informal processes is the company's structure based on? Shared Values: What is the idea the organization subscribes to? Is this idea communicated credibly to others? Staff: This element refers to employees development and relevant processes, performances and feedback programs etc. Skill: What is the company's base of skills and competencies? Style: This depicts the leadership style and how it influences the strategic decisions of the organization.**==

**The hard elements, in detail.** ==**The Hard elements are directly controlled by the management.**== ==**♦ Strategy: the direction of the organization, a blueprint to build on a core competency and achieve competitive advantage to drive margins and lead the industry. ♦ Structure: depending on the availability of resources and the degree of centralisation or decentralization that the management desires, it choses from the available alternatives of organizational structures. ♦ Systems: the development of daily tasks, operations and teams to execute the goals and objectives in the most efficient and effective manner.**==

**The soft elements, in detail.** ==**The Soft elements are difficult to define as they are more governed by the culture. But these soft elements are equally important in determining an organization's success as well as growth in the industry.**== ==**♦ Shared Values: The core values which get reflected within the organizational culture or influence the code of ethics of the management. ♦ Style: This depicts the leadership style and how it influences the strategic decisions of the organisation. It also revolves around people motivation and organizational delivery of goals. ♦ Staff: The talent pool of the organisation. ♦ Skills: The core competencies or the key skills of the employees play a vital role in defining the organizational success.**==

**The four limitations — three marks of a five-mark question.** ==**While the McKinsey 7S Model provides a structural approach to analyzing organizational effectiveness, it has certain limitations: ♦ It ignores the importance of the external environment and depicts only the most crucial elements within the organization. ♦ The model does not clearly explain the concept of organizational effectiveness or performance. ♦ The model is considered to be more static and less flexible for decision making. ♦ It is generally criticized for missing out the real gaps in conceptualization and execution of strategy.**==

**How to tell the elements apart in an MCQ — the discriminators ICAI actually uses.** **Systems** is named by **processes, platforms, protocols, appraisal mechanisms, information flow** (ICAI's Edu Edge answer: a centralised knowledge-sharing platform, defined communication protocols and appraisal linked to teamwork = **System**). **Style** is named by **how leaders interact with their teams and set examples for behaviour** (ICAI's Alpha Corp answer = **Style**). **Strategy** is named by **the deliberate use of a tool to attract or win customers** (ICAI's MuseoGoa answer: social media and pricing strategies to attract visitors = **Strategy**). **Skills** is named by **unfamiliarity with the technology, competency gaps**. **Staff** is the **talent pool**. **Structure** is **how work is divided**. **Shared Values** is **the idea the organization subscribes to**.

**Why the model belongs under 'Organizational Framework'.** The study material prints the 7S Model as §5.4 itself, with **§5.4.1 Organization Structure** and **§5.4.2 Organization Culture** as its two sub-headings. That is the chapter's own architecture: **Structure is the leading hard element and Culture is the leading soft element**, and the 7S is the frame that holds both. ICAI's closing sentence to §5.4.2 makes the point: ==**an excessive focus on the hard management, at best will result in a linear improvement in performance. On the other hand, performance can be improved exponentially by concentrating on the soft side of the management. The optimal management approach probably would be somewhere between these extremes.**==

**And the caution that closes the section.** ==**Every organisation has to maintain a fine balance between a range of "hard" and "soft" management as even though a structure is appropriate for the time it is established, by the time it is implemented, reality has already changed, especially in today's world.**==
concepts.example: A company that has run for a decade on its founder's values, in a limited area, now wants to leverage new skills in marketing, technology, product development and financial management — and knows that **modifying one aspect might have a ripple effect on other elements**. ICAI's answer: use the **McKinsey 7S Model** to analyse the organizational design, build the questionnaire from the three hard and four soft elements, and then state the model's four limitations. That is PYQ May 2024 Q5(a), marked 2 + 3 — two marks for the model, three for the limitations.

mistakes: **Putting Strategy among the soft elements.** It is **hard**, and ICAI has set an MCQ (May 2026 MCQ 10) whose whole point is that Strategy is not one of the soft elements that change during reinvention.

Giving three limitations instead of four. The fourth — **generally criticized for missing out the real gaps in conceptualization and execution of strategy** — is the one candidates drop, and in a 2 + 3 split it costs a mark.
Confusing **Systems** with **Structure**. Systems are **processes** — formal and informal, daily tasks and operations; Structure is **how work is divided** and how departments collaborate.

Confusing **Staff** with **Skills**. Staff is the **talent pool**; Skills are **the core competencies or the key skills of the employees**. A stem about employees being *unfamiliar with a technology* is Skills; a stem about *attracting and retaining* people is Staff.

Describing the soft elements as less important. The study material says they are **equally important in determining an organization's success as well as growth in the industry**, and that performance can be improved **exponentially** by concentrating on the soft side.
Forgetting the **ripple effect** sentence. When a stem includes it, the examiner is naming the model for you; when your answer includes it, you have shown you know the source.

official_questions.question: BOYA Ltd. is a venture in the market present for a decade. Till 2023 it was working on the values and vision of its founder while operating in a limited area of operations. Growth opportunities exist for BOYA Ltd. Considering the changing environment, the company is interested to leverage new skills in marketing, technology, product development and financial management. As a known fact, modifying one aspect might have a ripple effect on other elements. The company wants to understand the various hard and soft elements interrelated with each other in the company and having a bearing on effective operational results. As a strategist, you intend to prepare a questionnaire based on both types of elements by analyzing the organizational design. Briefly discuss the strategic model you will use in the given situation. State the limitations of the model as well. (2 + 3 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: **In addressing the strategic needs of BOYA Ltd., the McKinsey 7S Model is an effective tool to consider. This model focuses on the interaction of hard and soft elements within an organization, suggesting that modifying one aspect might have a ripple effect on the other elements to maintain an effective balance. The McKinsey 7S Model helps analyze the company's organizational design to achieve effectiveness through these interactions.**

**The model categorizes the elements into 'hard' and 'soft' components. The Hard elements are directly controlled by the management:** **Strategy — the direction of the organization, a blueprint to build on a core competency and achieve competitive advantage to drive margins and lead the industry; Structure — depending on the availability of resources and the degree of centralisation or decentralization that the management desires, it chooses from the available alternatives of organizational structures; Systems — the development of daily tasks, operations and teams to execute the goals and objectives in the most efficient and effective manner.**

**The Soft elements are difficult to define as they are more governed by the culture, but are equally important in determining an organization's success as well as growth:** **Shared Values, Style, Staff and Skills** — the core values and code of ethics; the leadership style and people motivation; the talent pool; and the core competencies or key skills of the employees.

**Because the question asks for a questionnaire, give ICAI's own framing questions:** **Strategy — what steps does the company intend to take to address current and future challenges? Structure — how is work divided, how do different departments work and collaborate? Systems — which formal and informal processes is the company's structure based on? Shared Values — what is the idea the organization subscribes to, and is this idea communicated credibly to others? Staff — employee development and relevant processes, performances and feedback programs. Skill — what is the company's base of skills and competencies? Style — the leadership style and how it influences the strategic decisions of the organization.**

**Limitations (the 3-mark limb): it ignores the importance of the external environment and depicts only the most crucial elements within the organization; the model does not clearly explain the concept of organizational effectiveness or performance; the model is considered to be more static and less flexible for decision making; and it is generally criticized for missing out the real gaps in conceptualization and execution of strategy.**

**Why the facts point to the 7S and nothing else:** the stem names **hard and soft elements**, the **ripple effect**, and the analysis of **organizational design** — all three are the model's own vocabulary. The founder's values moving to new skills in marketing, technology, product development and financial management is a shift in **Shared Values, Skills and Systems** together, which is precisely the interdependence the model exists to expose.

official_questions.question: York Investors, recognizing the importance of aligning its organizational elements with strategic objectives, has strategically invested in training programs, technology, and communication systems. The company aims to enhance the skills and capabilities of its workforce through comprehensive training initiatives. Simultaneously, York Investors leverages cutting-edge technology to streamline its operations and improve overall efficiency. The investment in communication systems ensures seamless collaboration and information flow across various departments. Identify and explain the model used by York Investors to achieve its strategic objectives. (ICAI's own label: Chapter 5)
answer_points: **York Investors is employing the McKinsey 7S Model to achieve its strategic objectives. The model focuses on seven interdependent elements within an organization, categorized into "Hard Ss" and "Soft Ss."**
**Strategy (Hard S): investing in training programs and technology aligns with the strategic objective of enhancing workforce skills and operational efficiency.**
**Structure (Hard S): the investment suggests a structural alignment to support the strategic initiatives, indicating a deliberate organization of resources.**

**Systems (Hard S): the use of cutting-edge technology and communication systems reflects a commitment to optimizing daily tasks and improving overall efficiency, addressing the system component of the model.**
**Shared Values (Soft S): the emphasis on comprehensive training initiatives indicates a commitment to shared values, reflecting a focus on developing a skilled and capable workforce.**

**Style (Soft S), Staff (Soft S) and Skills (Soft S):** the leadership style is implied in the strategic decision to invest in people; Staff is the talent pool being developed; and Skills — **the core competencies or the key skills of the employees** — are the direct object of the training programmes.
**ICAI's closing assessment:** **York Investors' approach demonstrates a holistic application of the McKinsey 7S Model, emphasizing the interconnectedness of both hard and soft elements.**

**Note the technique in ICAI's own answer** — it labels each element '(Hard S)' or '(Soft S)' as it goes. Copying that habit makes the three-and-four split visible to the examiner without spending a sentence on it.
also_asked_as: RTP-J25-SQ16 sets the same model for GloWare Ltd., an apparel manufacturer that until 2023 'operated on the founding principles of its CEO, focusing on a limited regional market' and now wants to develop new skills — the same facts as the BOYA Ltd. past-paper question. ICAI's answer there gives the model and then the four limitations, phrased as: **limited focus on external environment** ('the model focuses only on internal elements, potentially overlooking external factors impacting the organization'), **undefined organizational effectiveness** ('it does not clearly explain how to measure or achieve organizational effectiveness'), **static nature** ('the model is considered more static and may lack flexibility in dynamic decision-making situations') and **potential gaps in strategy execution** ('it may not fully capture gaps between strategy development and execution').

mcqs.question: Use McKinsey's 7S Model to identify the soft elements that change during reinvention: (i) Shared value (ii) Style (iii) Strategy (iv) Staff
mcqs.explanation: The soft elements are Shared Values, Style, Staff and Skills; the hard elements are Strategy, Structure and Systems. Of the four items listed, (i) Shared value, (ii) Style and (iv) Staff are soft, while (iii) Strategy is hard. ICAI key: (D).

why_wrong.A: It omits Staff, which is a soft element — 'the talent pool of the organisation'.
why_wrong.B: It includes Strategy, which the study material lists among the hard elements directly controlled by the management.
why_wrong.C: It includes Strategy, so it cannot be right.

mcqs.trap: The whole item exists to catch candidates who think Strategy must be soft because it involves judgement. Hard means **directly controlled by the management**, and a strategy document is exactly that.

mcqs.question: Edu Edge Learning, a digital education start-up, struggled with inconsistent communication and poor integration across departments. Although the strategy and talent were in place, collaboration was ineffective. To resolve this, the leadership launched a centralized knowledge-sharing platform and defined clear internal communication protocols. Performance appraisal systems were linked to teamwork and collaboration goals, ensuring alignment of all the processes with strategic intent. Which aspect of the McKinsey 7-S Framework is being strengthened at Edu Edge?
mcqs.explanation: Systems are 'the development of daily tasks, operations and teams to execute the goals and objectives in the most efficient and effective manner' and answer the question 'which formal and informal processes is the company's structure based on?' A knowledge-sharing platform, communication protocols and an appraisal mechanism are all processes. ICAI key: (C).

why_wrong.A: The stem says the strategy was already in place.
why_wrong.B: No change is made to how work is divided or how departments are constituted — only to the processes running between them.
why_wrong.D: The stem says the talent was already in place; nothing is done to the employees' competencies.

mcqs.trap: 'Poor integration across departments' sounds structural, which makes option B the live distractor. The remedies, though, are all processes, and the stem closes on **alignment of all the processes with strategic intent**.

mcqs.question: Alpha Corp is undergoing a shift to foster a culture that encourages innovative thinking and team collaboration. To achieve this, the company is focusing on how leaders interact with their teams and set examples for behaviour, aiming to align leadership practices with desired cultural outcomes. Which aspect of Alpha Corp is being adjusted to foster a culture of innovation and collaboration?
mcqs.explanation: Style 'depicts the leadership style and how it influences the strategic decisions of the organisation. It also revolves around people motivation and organizational delivery of goals' (SM §5.4). 'How leaders interact with their teams and set examples for behaviour' is the definition of Style. ICAI key: (d).

why_wrong.A: Structure concerns how work is divided and how departments collaborate formally.
why_wrong.B: Systems are the formal and informal processes.
why_wrong.C: Skills are the core competencies or key skills of the employees.

mcqs.trap: The stem mentions culture, which tempts Shared Values — not even offered as an option here, precisely because the examiner wants Style. The operative words are *leaders interact* and *set examples*.

mcqs.question: A financial services company wants to launch a mobile-first platform. The strategy is clearly defined and systems for operations are automated. However, employees are unfamiliar with the technology, and the leadership style emphasizes strict hierarchy, slowing down decision-making. Management wants to ensure the new digital initiative succeeds without resistance or delays. Which 7S elements need urgent alignment?
mcqs.explanation: The stem rules out two elements explicitly — the strategy is clear and the systems are automated — and then names two deficiencies: employees unfamiliar with the technology (**Skills**, 'the core competencies or the key skills of the employees') and a strict hierarchy slowing decisions (**Style**, 'the leadership style and how it influences the strategic decisions of the organisation'). ICAI key: (a).

why_wrong.B: No shortage of people is described, only of their competencies; and the structure is not said to be wrong.
why_wrong.C: Systems are stated to be automated already.
why_wrong.D: Strategy is stated to be clearly defined.

mcqs.trap: A strict hierarchy reads as a structural problem, which makes option B or D attractive. The study material files leadership behaviour under **Style**, not Structure — and the stem says the problem is the *style* that emphasises hierarchy.

mcqs.question: Why is the McKinsey 7S model significant in Swasthya's strategic management approach, and which elements of the model ensure a holistic alignment of their strategy?

options.A: It facilitates short-term profit maximization, with a focus on structure and style
options.B: It emphasizes a compartmentalized approach to strategy, focusing on shared values and skills
options.C: It ensures a comprehensive alignment of strategy, structure, systems, shared values, skills, style, and staff
options.D: It prioritizes immediate cost reduction by aligning systems and strategy

mcqs.explanation: The model's goal is 'to depict how effectiveness can be achieved in an organization through the interactions of hard and soft elements', and it works by showing that all seven are interrelated — so only an option naming all seven can be right. ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: The model is not about short-term profit, and it covers seven elements, not two.
why_wrong.B: The model is the opposite of compartmentalized — modifying one aspect has a ripple effect on the others.
why_wrong.D: Cost reduction is not the model's purpose.

mcqs.trap: Each wrong option names a real pair of elements, which makes them look technical; the giveaway is that the model's whole claim is interdependence across all seven.

mcqs.question: Which element of the 7S McKinsey model is demonstrated by MuseoGoa's strategic use of social media and pricing strategies to attract visitors?
mcqs.explanation: Strategy is 'the direction of the organization, a blueprint to build on a core competency and achieve competitive advantage', and answers 'what steps does the company intend to take to address current and future challenges?' The deliberate use of social media and pricing to win visitors is a strategic step. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: Style is the leadership style and how it influences strategic decisions.
why_wrong.C: Shared Values are the core values reflected in the culture or the code of ethics.
why_wrong.D: Skills are the employees' core competencies.

mcqs.trap: Marketing tactics feel operational rather than strategic; here they are the chosen means of competing, which is what the Strategy element covers.

mcqs.question: How does the application of the McKinsey 7S Model help Green Harvest Organics achieve its expansion objectives?

options.B: By aligning strategy, structure, systems, staff, skills, style and shared values to support organizational growth
options.C: By focusing only on marketing and branding initiatives

mcqs.explanation: The model's purpose is to depict how effectiveness is achieved through the interactions of all seven interrelated elements; it is a diagnostic and alignment tool, not a growth strategy. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: Developing new product lines is product development under Ansoff's matrix, SM Ch 4.
why_wrong.C: A focus on marketing alone is the opposite of a seven-element framework.
why_wrong.D: Entering international markets is market development, SM Ch 4.

mcqs.trap: Options A and D are both genuine growth strategies from SM Chapter 4, offered to see whether the candidate confuses a framework for analysing the organisation with a strategy for growing it.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a HARD element of the McKinsey 7S Model?
mcqs.explanation: The hard elements are Strategy, Structure and Systems — those 'directly controlled by the management'. The soft elements are Shared Values, Style, Staff and Skills, which 'are difficult to define as they are more governed by the culture'.

why_wrong.A: Shared Values is soft — the core values reflected in the culture or the code of ethics.
why_wrong.B: Staff is soft — the talent pool of the organisation.
why_wrong.C: Style is soft — the leadership style and how it influences strategic decisions.

mcqs.trap: All seven begin with S, which is the whole difficulty of the model; the split is three hard against four soft.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of the McKinsey 7S Model as stated in the study material?

options.A: It ignores the importance of the external environment
options.B: It is considered to be more static and less flexible for decision making
options.C: It applies only to manufacturing organisations and not to service firms
options.D: It is generally criticized for missing out the real gaps in conceptualization and execution of strategy

mcqs.explanation: The four limitations are: it ignores the external environment and depicts only the most crucial internal elements; it does not clearly explain the concept of organizational effectiveness or performance; it is more static and less flexible for decision making; and it misses the real gaps in conceptualization and execution of strategy. Sector is not among them.

mcqs.explanation: SM §5.4 defines Shared Values in exactly those words, and its questionnaire form of the element is 'What is the idea the organization subscribes to? Is this idea communicated credibly to others?'

why_wrong.B: Style depicts the leadership style and how it influences strategic decisions, and revolves around people motivation and organizational delivery of goals.
why_wrong.C: Strategy is the direction of the organization, a blueprint to build on a core competency.
why_wrong.D: Skills are the core competencies or the key skills of the employees.

mcqs.question: As per the study material's conclusion on hard and soft management, an excessive focus on hard management will:

options.A: At best result in a linear improvement in performance, whereas performance can be improved exponentially by concentrating on the soft side
options.B: Produce the fastest improvement, because hard elements are directly controlled by management
options.C: Have no effect, since only soft elements determine organizational success
options.D: Be the optimal approach in today's rapidly changing world

mcqs.explanation: SM §5.4.2's closing paragraph: 'an excessive focus on the hard management, at best will result in a linear improvement in performance. On the other hand, performance can be improved exponentially by concentrating on the soft side of the management. The optimal management approach probably would be somewhere between these extremes.'

why_wrong.B: Direct control is what makes them hard, but the study material rates the payoff as merely linear.
why_wrong.C: The study material calls for a fine balance, not for soft elements alone.
why_wrong.D: The optimal approach is said to be somewhere between the extremes.

recap: The 7S Model analyses organizational design to show how effectiveness is achieved through the interactions of hard and soft elements; modifying one has a ripple effect on the others.
Three hard elements, directly controlled by management: Strategy, Structure, Systems.
Four soft elements, governed by the culture and equally important: Shared Values, Style, Staff, Skills.
Four limitations: ignores the external environment; does not explain organizational effectiveness; more static and less flexible; misses the real gaps in conceptualization and execution.
MCQ discriminators: processes and platforms = Systems; how leaders interact = Style; the chosen means of competing = Strategy; employee competencies = Skills; the talent pool = Staff.
Excessive hard focus gives linear improvement; soft focus can give exponential improvement; the optimum lies between.

concepts.title: 5.4.1 Organization Structure — the eight types, and why structure follows strategy
concepts.evidence: PYQ 6 · RTP 6 · MTP 6 (18 atoms — the largest heading in the book)
understand: **Why strategy forces structural change — ICAI's two reasons.** ==**First, structure largely dictates how operational objectives and policies will be established to achieve the strategic objectives.**== ICAI's illustration: **objectives and policies established under a geographic organizational structure are couched in geographic terms; objectives and policies are stated largely in terms of products in an organization whose structure is based on product groups.** ==**The second major reason why changes in strategy often require changes in structure is that structure dictates how resources will be allocated to achieve strategic objectives.**== If the structure is by customer groups, resources are allocated that way; if by functional lines, by functional areas.

**Chandler.** ==**According to Chandler, changes in strategy lead to changes in organizational structure. Structure should be designed or redesigned to facilitate the strategic pursuit of a firm and, therefore, structure should follow strategy.**== **Chandler found a particular structure sequence to be often repeated as organizations grow and change strategy over time.** ==**There is no one optimal organizational design or structure for a given strategy. What is appropriate for one organization may not be appropriate for a similar firm, although successful firms in a given industry do tend to organize themselves in a similar way.**==

**The size progression — a reliable MCQ.** ==**Small firms tend to be functionally structured (centralized). Medium-size firms tend to be divisionally structured (decentralized). Large firms tend to use an SBU (strategic business unit) or matrix structure. As organizations grow, their structures generally change from simple to complex as a result of linking together of several basic strategies.**== ICAI adds: **consumer goods companies tend to emulate the divisional structure-by-product form of organization.**

**Chandler's Strategy-Structure Relationship, as the figure prints it:** ==**New strategy is formed → New administrative problems emerge → Organizational performance declines → A new organizational structure is established → Organizational performance improves**== — and round again. Note that performance *declines* before the new structure is built; that is the cycle's point.

**Symptoms of an ineffective organizational structure.** ==**Too many levels of management, too many meetings attended by too many people, too much attention being directed toward solving interdepartmental conflicts, too large a span of control, and too many unachieved objectives.**== ICAI's caution: **changes in organisational structure can facilitate strategy-implementation efforts, but changes in structure should not be expected to make a bad strategy good, to make bad managers good, or to make bad products sell.**

**Structure can also influence strategy — the backward linkage, again.** ==**If a proposed strategy required massive structural changes, it would not be an attractive choice. In this way, structure can shape the choice of strategy.**==

**What organizational structure is.** ==**Organizational structure is the company's formal configuration of its intended roles, procedures, governance mechanisms, authority, and decision-making processes.** **Organizational structure, influenced by factors such as an organization's age and size, acts as a framework which reflects managers' determination of what a company does and how tasks are completed, given the chosen strategy. The most important issue is that the company's structure must be congruent with or fit with the company's strategy.**==

**A — Simple Structure.** ==**Most appropriate for companies that follow a single-business strategy and offer a line of products in a single geographic market**, and **also appropriate for companies implementing focused cost leadership or focused differentiation strategies**. ==**An organizational form in which the owner-manager makes all major decisions directly and monitors all activities, while the company's staff merely serves as an executor.** Characterised by **little specialization of tasks, few rules, little formalization, unsophisticated information systems and direct involvement of owner-manager in all phases of day-to-day operations**. **Communication is frequent and direct, and new products tend to be introduced to the market quickly, which can result in a competitive advantage.** Its potential competitive advantages: **a broad-based openness to innovation, greater structural flexibility, and an ability to respond more rapidly to environmental changes.**== It is outgrown as information-processing requirements mount.

**B — Functional Structure.** ==**A widely used structure in business organisations… because of its simplicity and low cost. A functional structure groups tasks and activities by business function, such as production/operations, marketing, finance/accounting, research and development, and management information systems.**== ==**Besides being simple and inexpensive, a functional structure also promotes specialization of labour, encourages efficiency, minimizes the need for an elaborate control system, and allows rapid decision making.**== Its problems: ==**differences in functional specialization and orientation may impede communications and coordination**, and **functional specialists often may develop a myopic (or narrow) perspective, losing sight of the company's strategic vision and mission**== — which is cured by the multidivisional structure.

**C — Divisional Structure.** ==**Can be organized in one of the four ways: by geographic area, by product or service, by customer, or by process. With a divisional structure, functional activities are performed both centrally and in each division separately.**== **Advantages:** ==**accountability is clear — divisional managers can be held responsible for sales and profit levels**; based on **extensive delegation of authority**, so managers and employees **can easily see the results of their good or bad performances**; **employee morale is generally higher** than in a centralized structure; it **creates career development opportunities for managers, allows local control of local situations, leads to a competitive climate within an organization, and allows new businesses and products to be added easily**.== **Limitations:** ==**it is costly** — **each division requires functional specialists who must be paid**; **there exists some duplication of staff services, facilities, and personnel**; **managers must be well qualified because the divisional design forces delegation of authority**, and better-qualified individuals require higher salaries; it **requires an elaborate, headquarters-driven control system**; and **certain regions, products, or customers may sometimes receive special treatment**, making it **difficult to maintain consistent, companywide practices**.==

**The four divisional forms, each with its trigger.** **By geographic area** — for organizations whose **strategies are formulated to fit the particular needs and characteristics of customers in different geographic areas**, most appropriate where there are **similar branch facilities located in widely dispersed areas**; it **allows local participation in decision making and improved coordination within a region**. **By product or service** — **most effective when specific products or services need special emphasis**, or when the firm **offers only a few products** or its **products or services differ substantially**; it **allows strict control over and attention to product lines, but may require a more skilled management force and reduced top management control** (ICAI's examples: General Motors, DuPont, Procter & Gamble). **By customer** — **when a few major customers are of paramount importance and many different services are provided to these customers**; examples are book publishers organised around colleges, secondary schools and private commercial schools, airlines with passenger and freight divisions, and banks with personal and corporate banking. **By process** — **similar to a functional structure, because activities are organized according to the way work is actually performed**, but ==**a key difference between these two designs is that functional departments are not accountable for profits or revenues, whereas divisional process departments are evaluated on these criteria.**==

**D — Multi Divisional (M-form) Structure.** ==**Composed of operating divisions where each division represents a separate business to which the top corporate officer delegates responsibility for day-to-day operations and business unit strategy to division managers. By such delegation, the corporate office is responsible for formulating and implementing overall corporate strategy and manages divisions through strategic and financial controls.**== ==**Developed in the 1920s, in response to coordination- and control-related problems in large firms**== — functional departments struggled with distinct product lines, costs were not allocated to individual products so profit contribution could not be assessed, and **top managers became over-involved in solving short-run problems… and neglected long-term strategic issues**. ==**Multidivisional structure calls for: creating separate divisions, each representing a distinct business; each division would house its functional hierarchy; division managers would be given responsibility for managing day-to-day operations; and a small corporate office that would determine the long-term strategic direction of the firm and exercise overall financial control over the semi-autonomous divisions.**== ==**When the firm is less diversified, strategic controls are used to manage divisions… an increase in diversification strains corporate officers' abilities to understand the operations of all of its business units and divisions are then managed by financial controls**== — and because financial controls require each division's performance to be largely independent, ==**the Strategic Business Units come into picture**==.

**E — Strategic Business Unit (SBU) Structure.** ==**This concept is relevant to multi-product, multi-business enterprises. It is impractical for an enterprise with a multitude of businesses to provide separate strategic planning treatment to each one of its products/businesses; it has to necessarily group the products/businesses into a manageable number of strategically related business units and then take them up for strategic planning.**== ==**An SBU is a grouping of related businesses, which is amenable to composite planning treatment.**==

**The three most important characteristics of an SBU** — the single most examined list in this heading: ==**♦ It is a single business or a collection of related businesses which offer scope for independent planning and which might feasibly stand alone from the rest of the organization. ♦ It has its own set of competitors. ♦ It has a manager who has responsibility for strategic planning and profit performance, and who has control of profit-influencing factors.**==

**Why the SBU concept arose.** Historically large firms planned **on a territorial basis**, which created two difficulties: ==**(i) since a number of territorial units handled the same product, the same product was getting varied strategic planning treatments; and (ii) since a given territorial planning unit carried different and unrelated products, products with dissimilar characteristics were getting identical strategic planning treatment.**== The SBU concept breaks away from that: **just because a firm is structured into a number of territorial units, say six units, it is not necessarily in six different businesses.** ==**A strategic business unit (SBU) structure consists of at least three levels, with a corporate headquarters at the top, SBU groups at the second level, and divisions grouped by relatedness within each SBU at the third level.**== **Within each SBU, divisions are related to each other, as also that SBU groups are unrelated to each other**, and **individual SBUs are treated as profit centres and controlled by corporate headquarters.** ICAI's example: **Sony has been restructuring to match the SBU structure with its ten SBUs.**

**The attributes of an SBU and the benefits of the SBU structure** — ICAI's own list, which is what the PQR Ltd. case asks for: ==**♦ A scientific method of grouping the businesses of a multi-business corporation which helps the firm in strategic planning. ♦ An improvement over the territorial grouping of businesses and strategic planning based on territorial units. ♦ An SBU is a grouping of related businesses that can be taken up for strategic planning distinct from the rest of the businesses; products/businesses within an SBU receive same strategic planning treatment and priorities. ♦ The task consists of analysing and segregating the assortment of businesses/portfolios and regrouping them into a few, well defined, distinct, scientifically demarcated business units; products/businesses that are related from the standpoint of "function" are assembled together as a distinct SBU. ♦ Unrelated products/businesses in any group are separated. ♦ Grouping the businesses on SBU lines helps the firm in strategic planning by removing the vagueness and confusion generally seen in grouping businesses; it also facilitates the right setting for correct strategic planning and facilitates correct relative priorities and resources to the various businesses. ♦ Each SBU is a separate business from the strategic planning standpoint; in the basic factors, viz., mission, objectives, competition and strategy, one SBU will be distinct from another. ♦ Each SBU will have its own distinct set of competitors and its own distinct strategy. ♦ Each SBU will have a CEO, responsible for strategic planning for the SBU and its profit performance, with control over most of the factors affecting its profit.**==

**The three ways relatedness can exist across SBUs** — ICAI's Unilever illustration: ==**SBUs might build on similar technologies, or all provide similar sorts of products or services. SBUs might be serving similar or different markets — even if technology or products differ, it may be that the customers are similar** (the technologies behind frozen food, washing powders and margarine are very different, **but all are sold through retail operations**). **Or it may be that other competences on which the competitive advantage of different SBUs are built have similarities** — Unilever would argue the marketing skills across the three product markets are similar.==

**F — Matrix Structure.** ==**May be very appropriate when organizations conclude that neither functional nor divisional forms, even when combined with horizontal linking mechanisms like strategic business units, are right for the implementation of their strategies. In matrix structure, functional and product forms are combined simultaneously at the same level of the organization. Employees have two superiors, a product or project manager and a functional manager.**== **The "home" department — engineering, manufacturing, or marketing — is usually functional and is reasonably permanent; people from these functional units are often assigned temporarily to one or more product units or projects**, which are **usually temporary and act like divisions in that they are differentiated on a product-market basis**.

==**A matrix structure is the most complex of all designs because it depends upon both vertical and horizontal flows of authority and communication (hence the term matrix).**== It **can result in higher overhead because it has more management positions**, and its other complexity drivers are ==**dual lines of budget authority (a violation of the unity command principle), dual sources of reward and punishment, shared authority, dual reporting channels, and a need for an extensive and effective communication system**==. **Advantages:** ==**project objectives are clear, there are many channels of communication, workers can see the visible results of their work, and shutting down a project is accomplished relatively easily**==. **Requirements for effectiveness:** ==**planning, training, clear mutual understanding of roles and responsibilities, excellent internal communication, and mutual trust and confidence**==. ICAI notes it **was developed to combine the stability of the functional structure with the flexibility of the product form**, is **very useful when the external environment (especially its technological and market aspects) is very complex and changeable**, but **produces conflicts revolving around duties, authority, and resource allocation**, and **is not very popular because of difficulties in implementation and trouble in managing**. **The three conditions under which it is found:** ==**1) Ideas need to be cross-fertilised across projects or products, 2) Resources are scarce and 3) Abilities to process information and to make decisions need to be improved.**==

**G — Network Structure.** ==**A radical organizational design, the network structure is an example of what could be termed a "non-structure" by its virtual elimination of in-house business functions. Many activities are outsourced. A corporation organized in this manner is often called a virtual organization because it is composed of a series of project groups or collaborations linked by constantly changing non-hierarchical, cobweb-like networks.**== ==**The network structure becomes most useful when the environment of a firm is unstable and is expected to remain so. Under such conditions, there is usually a strong need for innovation and quick response.**== **Instead of having salaried employees, it may contract with people for a specific project or length of time; long-term contracts with suppliers and distributors replace services that the company could provide for itself through vertical integration.** ==**The organization is, in effect, only a shell, with a small headquarters acting as a "broker", electronically connected to some completely owned divisions, partially owned subsidiaries, and other independent organisations.**== ICAI's example: **companies like Airtel use the network structure in their operations function by subcontracting manufacturing to other companies in low-cost** locations.

**The network's merits and demerits.** ==**It provides an organization with increased flexibility and adaptability to cope with rapid technological change and shifting patterns of international trade and competition. It allows a company to concentrate on its distinctive competencies, while gathering efficiencies from other firms who are concentrating their efforts in their areas of expertise.**== ==**Disadvantages: the availability of numerous potential partners can be a source of trouble; contracting out functions to separate suppliers/distributors may keep the firm from discovering any synergies by combining activities; and if a particular firm over specialises on only a few functions, it runs the risk of choosing the wrong functions and thus becoming non-competitive.**==

**H — Hourglass Structure.** ==**In recent years information technology and communications have significantly altered the functioning of organizations. The role played by middle management is diminishing as the tasks performed by them are increasingly being replaced by the technological tools. Hourglass organization structure consists of three layers with constricted middle layer. The structure has a short and narrow middle-management level. Information technology links the top and bottom levels in the organization taking away many tasks that are performed by the middle level managers. A shrunken middle layer coordinates diverse lower-level activities. Contrary to traditional middle level managers who are often specialist, the managers in the hourglass structure are generalists and perform wide variety of tasks. They would be handling cross-functional issues emanating such as those from marketing, finance or production.**==

**The hourglass trade-off.** ==**Hourglass structure has obvious benefit of reduced costs. It also helps in enhancing responsiveness by simplifying decision making. Decision making authority is shifted close to the source of information so that it is faster. However, with the reduced size of middle management the promotion opportunities for the lower levels diminish significantly. Continuity at same level may bring monotony and lack of interest and it becomes difficult to keep the motivation levels high. Organisations try to overcome these problems by assigning challenging tasks, transferring laterally and having a system of proper rewards for performance.**==

mistakes: **Confusing Divisional, Multi-divisional and SBU.** All three have divisions with their own heads. **Divisional**: functional activities performed both centrally and in each division separately, organised by area, product, customer or process. **M-form**: each division a separate business, with **a small corporate office** setting long-term direction and exercising **overall financial control**. **SBU**: *related* businesses grouped for **composite strategic planning**, each with **its own set of competitors** and its own CEO. In MCQs the phrase 'its own set of competitors' is the SBU giveaway.

Giving two SBU characteristics instead of three. The three are independent planning scope, its own set of competitors, and a manager with responsibility for strategic planning and profit performance **and control of profit-influencing factors**.

Saying the matrix has one boss with dotted-line reporting. **Employees have two superiors, a product or project manager and a functional manager**, and the structure involves **dual lines of budget authority (a violation of the unity command principle)**.

The benefit is reduced cost and faster decisions; the cost is that **promotion opportunities for the lower levels diminish significantly**, risking **monotony and lack of interest**, countered by **challenging tasks, lateral transfers and proper rewards for performance**.

Writing that structural change can fix a bad strategy. ICAI says the opposite: **changes in structure should not be expected to make a bad strategy good, to make bad managers good, or to make bad products sell.**

Missing the divisional-process versus functional distinction: **functional departments are not accountable for profits or revenues, whereas divisional process departments are evaluated on these criteria.**

official_questions.question: A Mumbai-based conglomerate, PQR Ltd., has announced a major restructuring of its business operations. official_questions.question: ABC group of companies has five projects at different geographical locations. Each project is managed by a dedicated project manager. A Chief Executive Officer is supported by a team of subject matter experts (SMEs) in each function at corporate level. As an accepted practice, the authority and communication flow vertically and horizontally in the company. There are five common functions — finance, human resource, operations, marketing and information technology — facilitating each project. Each functional manager has an administrative relationship with the respective project manager and a functional relationship with the related SME, with a clear mutual understanding of his or her roles and responsibilities. Identify and explain the organizational structure best suited in the above scenario. State the advantages and disadvantages of the structure. (1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: **The organizational structure best suited for the ABC group of companies is the Matrix Structure.**

**The Matrix Structure integrates functional and project-based frameworks, enabling vertical communication between functional managers and teams, and horizontal communication with project managers. Functional managers oversee domains and report to SMEs, while project managers handle project execution. This structure ensures resource sharing, role clarity, collaboration, and alignment with organizational objectives.**

**Advantages:** **Resource Optimization — efficient utilization of resources across multiple projects.** **Flexibility — shutting down a project is accomplished relatively easily because it quickly adapts to changes in project needs or external environments.** **Enhanced Communication — it encourages collaboration**, there being **many channels of communication**, and **project objectives are clear** with **workers able to see the visible results of their work**.

**Disadvantages:** the matrix is **the most complex of all designs because it depends upon both vertical and horizontal flows of authority and communication**; it **can result in higher overhead because it has more management positions**; and it brings **dual lines of budget authority (a violation of the unity command principle), dual sources of reward and punishment, shared authority, dual reporting channels, and a need for an extensive and effective communication system**.

**Add the conflict point:** the structure **produces conflicts revolving around duties, authority, and resource allocation**, and **to the extent that the goals to be achieved are vague and the technology used is poorly understood, a continuous battle for power between product and functional managers is likely.** It **is not very popular because of difficulties in implementation and trouble in managing.**

**Why the facts can only be a matrix:** the stem says **authority and communication flow vertically and horizontally** — the definition of the term — and gives each functional manager **two relationships**, administrative to the project manager and functional to the SME. That is ICAI's **two superiors** condition. The 'clear mutual understanding of roles and responsibilities' is also lifted from the study material's list of what a matrix needs to be effective.

Note the four-way mark split — **1 for identification, 2 for the explanation, 1 for advantages, 1 for disadvantages** — so a candidate who names the structure and explains it but omits either list loses a fifth of the marks.

While eliminating in-house business functions, the company is considering outsourcing major activities and focusing on its core competencies. Identify the organizational structure suitable for the company, and outline the merits and demerits of the identified structure. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **The suitable organizational structure for MTS Ltd. is the Network Organizational Structure. A company with such a structure is often called a Virtual Organization.**

**Merit — Flexibility and Adaptability: the structure allows for rapid technological changes and shifting competition patterns. This enables the company to adapt quickly to the unstable environment and changing customer preferences.**
**Merit — Focus on Core Competencies: the company can concentrate on its distinctive competencies while outsourcing non-core functions to specialized firms, which can perform them more efficiently.**
**Merit — Cost Efficiency: through subcontracting and outsourcing, MTS Ltd. can reduce the costs associated with maintaining in-house teams.**

**Merit — Decentralized Operations: the network structure scatters business functions across various geographical locations, reducing the need for a large central headquarters and ensuring responsiveness.**

**Demerits, from the study material:** **the availability of numerous potential partners can be a source of trouble**; **contracting out functions to separate suppliers/distributors may keep the firm from discovering any synergies by combining activities**; and **if a particular firm over specialises on only a few functions, it runs the risk of choosing the wrong functions and thus becoming non-competitive**.

**Why the facts point here:** three of the study material's own trigger conditions appear in the stem — **the environment of a firm is unstable and is expected to remain so**, **a strong need for innovation and quick response**, and the **virtual elimination of in-house business functions** through outsourcing. Note also that **long-term contracts with suppliers and distributors replace services that the company could provide for itself through vertical integration** — which is why a network is the alternative to the Chapter 4 integration route.

official_questions.question: Write a short note on the hourglass organizational structure. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **In recent years information technology and communications have significantly altered the functioning of organizations. The role played by middle management is diminishing as the tasks performed by them are increasingly being replaced by the technological tools.**
**Hourglass organization structure consists of three layers with a constricted middle layer. The structure has a short and narrow middle-management level.**

**Information technology links the top and bottom levels in the organization, taking away many tasks that are performed by the middle level managers. A shrunken middle layer coordinates diverse lower-level activities.**

**Contrary to traditional middle level managers who are often specialist, the managers in the hourglass structure are generalists and perform a wide variety of tasks. They would be handling cross-functional issues emanating such as those from marketing, finance or production.**

**Benefits: the hourglass structure has the obvious benefit of reduced costs. It also helps in enhancing responsiveness by simplifying decision making. Decision making authority is shifted close to the source of information so that it is faster.**

**Drawback: however, with the reduced size of middle management the promotion opportunities for the lower levels diminish significantly. Continuity at same level may bring monotony and lack of interest and it becomes difficult to keep the motivation levels high.**
**The remedy: organisations try to overcome these problems by assigning challenging tasks, transferring laterally and having a system of proper rewards for performance.**
A 5-mark short note needs all four limbs — what it is, why it has arisen, what it gains, and what it costs with the remedy. The specialist-to-generalist shift is the detail most candidates omit.

three layers with constricted middle layer
links the top and bottom levels
close to the source of information

mcqs.question: Super Products Ltd. has four divisions — Alpha, Beta, Cos and Theta. All the divisions are independent product centres and are also an integral part of the company's product Gama. Each division contains its own set of activities under the control of a respective general manager, who is responsible for his respective product line and its profitability. While having its own set of competitors, each centre has its own competitive advantages with the resources and capabilities they develop. Such a structure is known as:
mcqs.explanation: Three of the SBU's defining features appear in the stem: a collection of related businesses offering scope for independent planning; **its own set of competitors**; and a manager with responsibility for the product line and its **profit performance** who controls the profit-influencing factors. ICAI key: (D).

why_wrong.A: A network structure outsources in-house functions and operates as a shell with a broker headquarters.
why_wrong.B: A divisional structure is organised by geography, product, customer or process, with functional activities performed both centrally and in each division — it carries no requirement of its own competitors.
why_wrong.C: The M-form delegates day-to-day operations with a small corporate office exercising financial control; the stem's emphasis on each centre's own competitors and own competitive advantages points past it to the SBU.

mcqs.trap: Options B, C and D are three steps of the same evolutionary ladder and all three fit a loose reading. The discriminator ICAI plants every time is **'its own set of competitors'**, which is the second of the SBU's three characteristics.

mcqs.question: M/s. SPG is a multi-product, multi-business enterprise. It has four prominent divisions. Each division functions as an independent product centre with its own set of activities managed by the respective division head, who is responsible for its own performance and profitability. This organizational structure is known as:
mcqs.explanation: The SBU concept 'is relevant to multi-product, multi-business enterprises', and the stem uses that phrase outright. Each division is an independent product centre with a head responsible for performance and profitability — the SBU's third characteristic. ICAI key: (C).

why_wrong.A: A divisional structure need not be multi-business, and its divisions are not necessarily independent planning units.
why_wrong.B: The M-form's distinguishing feature is the small corporate office exercising financial control, which the stem does not mention.

mcqs.trap: 'Multi-product, multi-business' is the SBU section's own opening phrase, so a candidate who has read §5.4.1's heading E answers in seconds — and one who has not is left choosing between four plausible structures.

mcqs.question: Innovexa Solutions Ltd. operates in the technology sector and has four divisions: Innovate, Develop, Transform and Elevate. Each division functions as an independent product centre while also contributing to the company's flagship product, TechSphere. Every division has its own set of activities, managed by a respective division head who is responsible for the product line's performance and profitability. While competing in different market segments, each division leverages its own unique resources and capabilities to maintain a competitive edge. This type of organizational structure is known as:
mcqs.explanation: Independent product centres, each with a head accountable for profit performance, each competing in its own market segment with its own resources and capabilities — the SBU's three characteristics. ICAI key: (d).

why_wrong.A: No outsourcing or contracting is described.
why_wrong.B: A divisional structure performs functional activities both centrally and in each division; it does not require separate competitive arenas.
why_wrong.C: The M-form is defined by its small corporate office and financial controls.

mcqs.trap: This is the Super Products and SPG item restaged a third time with different names — a reminder that the examiner reuses the same discriminators. 'Competing in different market segments' is 'its own set of competitors'.

mcqs.question: Jayant oversees the 'Consumer Goods' segment of a large conglomerate. This specific segment has its own dedicated legal and finance heads who operate semi-autonomously from other segments like 'Industrial Parts'. This structure is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: A segment grouping related businesses, with its own functional heads operating semi-autonomously from unrelated segments, is an SBU: 'within each SBU, divisions are related to each other, as also that SBU groups are unrelated to each other', and individual SBUs are treated as profit centres. ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: A simple structure has an owner-manager making all major decisions directly, with little formalization.
why_wrong.B: A matrix would give employees two superiors, a functional and a project manager.
why_wrong.D: A functional structure groups the whole company by business function under one chief executive, not by segment.

mcqs.trap: 'Dedicated legal and finance heads' sounds functional, which makes option D tempting; the functions are dedicated *to the segment*, which is the opposite of a functional structure.

mcqs.question: Horizon Technologies implemented a Strategic Business Unit (SBU) structure to improve its responsiveness and innovation. How did the SBU structure differ from the company's previous organizational model, and what benefits did this new structure bring?

options.A: The SBU structure replaced a functional structure and empowered units to make strategic decisions, leading to quicker market responsiveness
options.B: The SBU structure replaced a matrix structure and centralised all strategic decisions at corporate headquarters
options.C: The SBU structure eliminated the need for any corporate headquarters
options.D: The SBU structure removed divisional profit accountability in favour of company-wide targets

mcqs.explanation: The study material's progression is functional for small firms, divisional for medium and SBU or matrix for large, and an SBU has 'a manager who has responsibility for strategic planning and profit performance, and who has control of profit-influencing factors' — so the move empowers the units. ICAI key: (a).

why_wrong.B: An SBU structure decentralises strategic planning to the SBU's own CEO rather than centralising it.
why_wrong.C: An SBU structure has at least three levels, with a corporate headquarters at the top.
why_wrong.D: Individual SBUs are treated as profit centres, so profit accountability is strengthened, not removed.

mcqs.trap: Options C and D each invert a real feature of the structure — the three-level shape and profit-centre treatment — which is how the examiner tests whether the characteristics were learned or merely recognised.

mcqs.question: What organizational structure is best suited for House of Jani's strategic need for dynamic allocation of resources, ensuring each project and department is mentored, monitored and maximized via multiple leaders?
mcqs.explanation: 'Via multiple leaders' is the matrix's defining feature — 'employees have two superiors, a product or project manager and a functional manager' — and the structure is found where 'resources are scarce' and must be allocated dynamically across projects. ICAI key: (b).

why_wrong.A: A functional structure has a single vertical line of authority through the functional head.
why_wrong.C: An hourglass structure is about a constricted middle-management layer, not multiple reporting lines.
why_wrong.D: A network structure outsources functions to external partners.

mcqs.trap: 'Dynamic allocation of resources' could describe several structures; 'multiple leaders' settles it, because only the matrix gives an employee two superiors.

mcqs.question: Hepha.io's initial structure, characterized by a highly dispersed team of scholars, relies heavily on coordination through technology and contracts. This structural design is most accurately identified as:
mcqs.explanation: A dispersed organisation coordinated by technology and contracts is the network structure — 'instead of having salaried employees, it may contract with people for a specific project or length of time', with the firm 'only a shell, with a small headquarters acting as a broker, electronically connected' to its parts. ICAI key: (c).

why_wrong.A: A divisional structure groups by geography, product, customer or process with functional activities performed centrally and divisionally.
why_wrong.B: A matrix combines functional and product forms at the same level with two superiors; no dual reporting is described.
why_wrong.D: An SBU groups related businesses for composite strategic planning, each with its own competitors.

mcqs.trap: 'Highly dispersed' could read as geographic divisionalisation; the giveaway is **contracts** rather than employees, and **technology** rather than hierarchy.

mcqs.question: The role played by middle management is diminishing as the tasks performed by them are increasingly being replaced by new and improved technological tools. As a result, in a three-layer organizational structure, the middle level is constricted. Which one of the following is a suitable name for such a structure?
mcqs.explanation: SM §5.4.1, heading H: 'Hourglass organization structure consists of three layers with constricted middle layer. The structure has a short and narrow middle-management level. Information technology links the top and bottom levels in the organization taking away many tasks that are performed by the middle level managers.' ICAI key: (A).

why_wrong.B: A network structure virtually eliminates in-house functions and outsources them.
why_wrong.C: A matrix combines functional and product forms at the same level, giving employees two superiors.
why_wrong.D: A divisional structure is organised by geography, product, customer or process.

mcqs.trap: The stem is the study material's own paragraph with the name removed — which makes it one of the easiest two marks in the paper, provided heading H was read.

mcqs.question: As per the study material, medium-size firms tend to be:

options.B: Organised as networks, to keep overheads low

mcqs.explanation: SM §5.4.1: 'Small firms tend to be functionally structured (centralized). Medium-size firms tend to be divisionally structured (decentralized). Large firms tend to use an SBU (strategic business unit) or matrix structure.'

why_wrong.B: The network structure is driven by environmental instability and the need for innovation and quick response, not by firm size.

mcqs.trap: Three of the four options are true statements about *some* size of firm; only one matches 'medium'.

mcqs.question: What is the key difference the study material draws between a divisional structure by process and a functional structure?

options.A: Divisional process departments are accountable for profits or revenues, whereas functional departments are not
options.B: A divisional process structure is used only by service firms
options.C: A functional structure organises activities according to the way work is actually performed, while a divisional process structure does not
options.D: A divisional process structure gives employees two superiors

mcqs.explanation: SM §5.4.1: 'A divisional structure by process is similar to a functional structure, because activities are organized according to the way work is actually performed. However, a key difference between these two designs is that functional departments are not accountable for profits or revenues, whereas divisional process departments are evaluated on these criteria.'

why_wrong.B: The study material makes no such restriction.
why_wrong.C: Both organise activities by the way work is performed — that is the stated similarity.
why_wrong.D: Two superiors is the matrix structure's feature.

mcqs.trap: Option C states the similarity as if it were the difference, which is the natural mis-reading of a sentence that begins by noting that the two designs are alike.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT listed by the study material as a symptom of an ineffective organizational structure?

options.A: Too large a span of control
options.B: Too many meetings attended by too many people
options.C: Too much attention being directed toward solving interdepartmental conflicts
options.D: A high ratio of variable to fixed cost

mcqs.explanation: The symptoms listed are: too many levels of management; too many meetings attended by too many people; too much attention directed toward solving interdepartmental conflicts; too large a span of control; and too many unachieved objectives. Cost structure is not among them.

why_wrong.A: It is the fourth symptom listed.
why_wrong.B: It is the second.

mcqs.trap: A cost ratio sounds like an organisational diagnostic, and it is a real concept elsewhere in the paper (operating leverage in FM) — but not in this list.

mcqs.question: In Chandler's strategy-structure relationship as the study material prints it, what happens immediately after new administrative problems emerge?

options.A: A new organizational structure is established

mcqs.explanation: The printed cycle runs: new strategy is formed → new administrative problems emerge → **organizational performance declines** → a new organizational structure is established → organizational performance improves. The decline is what forces the restructuring.

why_wrong.A: The new structure comes after the decline, not before it.
why_wrong.B: Performance improves only once the new structure is in place.
why_wrong.D: The new strategy starts the cycle.

mcqs.trap: It is tempting to assume a well-run firm restructures as soon as problems appear; Chandler's observation is that the performance dip is what triggers the change.

mcqs.question: Which statement about organization structure is INCORRECT as per the study material?

options.A: Structure should be designed or redesigned to facilitate the strategic pursuit of a firm, so structure should follow strategy
options.B: Changes in structure can be expected to make a bad strategy good and bad products sell
options.C: There is no one optimal organizational design or structure for a given strategy
options.D: If a proposed strategy required massive structural changes, it would not be an attractive choice

mcqs.explanation: The study material says the opposite: 'changes in organisational structure can facilitate strategy-implementation efforts, but changes in structure should not be expected to make a bad strategy good, to make bad managers good, or to make bad products sell.'

why_wrong.A: That is Chandler's proposition as the study material states it.
why_wrong.C: Verbatim — successful firms in an industry do tend to organise similarly, but there is no single optimum.
why_wrong.D: Verbatim — this is how structure can shape the choice of strategy.

mcqs.trap: Restructuring is so often presented as a cure that option B reads as orthodoxy; ICAI explicitly disclaims it.

recap: Chandler: changes in strategy lead to changes in structure, so structure should follow strategy — but structure also shapes which strategies are attractive.
Size rule: small = functional and centralized; medium = divisional and decentralized; large = SBU or matrix.
The eight types: Simple, Functional, Divisional (by area, product, customer or process), Multi-divisional (M-form), SBU, Matrix, Network, Hourglass.

An SBU's three characteristics: a single or collection of related businesses that could stand alone; its own set of competitors; a manager responsible for strategic planning and profit performance with control of profit-influencing factors. At least three levels, treated as profit centres.
A matrix combines functional and product forms at the same level, giving two superiors; it is the most complex design, with dual budget authority violating unity of command.

A network is a 'non-structure' — a shell with a broker headquarters, for unstable environments; an hourglass has a constricted middle layer of generalist managers, cheaper and faster but with fewer promotions.
